15137.title: Al-Kindī: The Founder of Philosophical Exegesis of the Qur'an
15137.abstract: Al-Kindī is well known as the first great ‘Islamic philosopher’. In contrast to his eminent successors, i.e. al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā and Ibn Rushd, he adhered to the idea of a creation in time, not to that of the eternity of the world. He appears to have made this choice out of religious motives: certainly he did find support in the philosophical arguments of Philoponus, but one is inclined to believe that he accepted this point of view because of what revelation tells on this issue. However, in those works of his that have reached us, one finds almost no references to the Qur'an. 1378.abstract: Kıraat ilmi, Kur’ân-ı Kerîm’i konu edinmesi sebebiyle diğer şer‘î ilimlerle doğrudan ilişkilidir. Bu noktada i‘râb ilmi ise kıraat ilminin bir ortağı olarak öne çıkmaktadır. 21320.title: Majaz dalam al-Quran: Refleksi atas Persoalan Linguistik / Majaz in the Koran: Reflection on Linguistic issues / Al-Majaz fi al-Qur’an: Al-Taammul fi Qadhaya Lughawiyah
21320.authors: Abd Fattah, Hamzah Hamzah, M. Napis Djuaeni, M. Abdul Hamid
21320.journal: Ijaz Arabi Journal of Arabic Learning
21320.abstract: Secara historis, tidak semua ulama menerima keberadaan makna majazi dalam al-Quran. Hal tersebut menjadi suatu hal kontroversial dikalangan para ulama bahasa dan mufassir dengan dalih masing-masing. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk merefleksikan persoalan linguistik terhadap makna majazi dalam al-Qurán dengan sub bahasan terminologi majaz dan klasifikasinya dalam ilmu Balaghah, pro-kontra eksistensi majaz dalam al-Quran, dan contoh kalimat majazi dalam al-Quran. Penelitian ini termasuk dalam penelitian deskriptif kualitatif yang desainnya termasuk studi pustaka sebab data-datanya berasal dari berbagai referensi pustaka baik berbentuk buku maupun artikel ilmiah. 14126.title: Development of a Jamʿ al-Āyāt Procedure in Mawḍūʿī Tafsir: An Integrated Model of Syntagmatic Analysis, Tafsir Verification, and Corpus Selection
14126.authors: Yedi Kuswandi, Dalpa Rahmawati, Desi Hasninadia, Irma Riyani
14126.abstract: Verse collection (jamʿ al-āyāt) is the second of seven steps in al-Farmāwī's mawḍūʿī tafsir, but the step does not specify how the thematic relevance of an individual candidate verse is to be assessed once it has been identified. This article develops a four-stage procedure — textual and syntagmatic analysis, preliminary thematic evaluation, tafsir verification, and synthesis and position determination — that operationalizes this step while keeping it within al-Farmāwī's seven-step framework. 12018.authors: Andhiarizqi Mulyawan, Yudianto Achmad, Zakaria Husin Lubis, Ahmad Kamaluddin
12018.abstract: The Qur'an's Natural Phenomena (Āyāt Kauniyyah) verses contain scientific clues, including one on seed-bearing plant morphology. 4791.title: CLASSIFICATION OF QURANIC VERSES INTERPRETED DISPUTATIOUSLY
4791.journal: The Journal of Interdisciplinary Human Studies
4791.abstract: This article examines the phenomenon of the disputatious or misinterpretation of Quranic verses by deviant movements and extremist groups throughout Islamic history and in the contemporary era. The study identifies the principal causes of misinterpretation including religious illiteracy, malicious ideological intent, and hyper-literalism and classifies the most commonly misused categories of Quranic verses. Specific cases are analysed: the use of Surah Ali ‘Imran 3:104 by Hizb ut-Tahrir to justify a political movement; the use of Surah an-Najm 53:39 to deny the transmission of spiritual reward to the deceased; the use of Surah al-An’am 6:57 and al-Ma’idah 5:44 by Kharijite-inspired groups to…

2461.title: Islām – Midrashic Perspectives on a Quranic Term
2461.abstract: Abstract The article examines several Quranic passages which contain the verb aslama and the noun islām in light of Jewish parallels. It is argued that these passages (Q 2:124–33; Q 37:84, 101-3; Q 27:29-44; Q 6:125) reflect midrashic traditions, and that the Arabic aslama and islām in these passages parallel the Hebrew be-lev shalem or hishlim. The latter term accrued two meanings: (1) to worship the Lord wholeheartedly (i.e., exclusively), and (2) to deliver one’s soul (to God) while accepting his authority and surrendering to him.
